identification.summary: TempTick is the FireEye (TEMP.) designation for an espionage actor that other sources track as Tick, also called Bronze Butler [S1][S2]. FireEye linked TEMP.Tick to a malicious Microsoft Word document in early May 2018 (per Korean press coverage [S8]), within a period of increased Chinese and Russian espionage against South Korea before the Trump-Kim summit [S2]. Secureworks (as Bronze Butler) and ESET (as Tick) describe a group that mainly targets Japanese organizations [S3][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Korean coverage of FireEye's 2018 findings says active since 2009 [S8]; Secureworks reporting says Japanese targeting since at least 2012 [S3].
identification.notes: The encyclopedia name TempTick is a FireEye-era label; later vendor reporting uses Tick or Bronze Butler [S1][S3][S5]. Search-result summaries of CFR's entry list Bronze Butler, RedBaldKnight and TAG-74 as related names [S1]. Cluster boundaries across vendors (FireEye TEMP.Tick, Secureworks Bronze Butler, ESET Tick, Sophos Bronze Butler) were not independently reconciled here; treat name equivalence as the cited sources' assertion.

attribution.sponsor: China (assessed). Secureworks assesses Bronze Butler likely originates in the People's Republic of China [S3]. FireEye assessed TEMP.Tick as Chinese-based per press coverage [S8].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only: Secureworks 'likely' PRC origin [S3]; FireEye assessed Chinese origin [S8]; ESET attributed the 2023 DLP-vendor intrusion to Tick with high confidence [S5]; Sophos describes the 2025 activity as China-linked [S6][S7]. No government attribution was verified in this research.
attribution.basis: Targeting that aligns with Chinese intelligence interests and long-running tooling and victim overlap across vendors [S3][S4][S5].

objectives: Espionage and theft of intellectual property and confidential data from Japanese and South Korean organizations [S3][S5].

sectors: Defense and military customers (via DLP vendor) [S5]
South Korean government ministries and financial institutions (broader 2018 targeting in FireEye reporting, not all attributed to TEMP.Tick) [S2]
Japanese companies using Lanscope Endpoint Manager [S6][S7]
targeting.notes: Search-result summaries of the CFR entry describe finance, defense, aerospace, technology, health-care, automotive and East Asian media targets; this list was not verified from the full page [S1]. Sophos stated 2025 exploitation was limited to sectors aligned with the actor's intelligence objectives [S6].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with weaponized Office documents [S2] and strategic web compromise; a Flash zero-day (CVE-2016-7836) used against SKYSEA Client View; Daserf backdoor with encrypted C2 [S3]. Trend Micro found Daserf variants using steganography and reports functions including shell execution, file transfer, screenshots and keylogging [S4]. In the 2023 ESET case the group compromised a DLP vendor's internal update servers and trojanized installers, using ShadowPy, Netboy (Invader) and Ghostdown [S5]. In 2025 Sophos reports zero-day exploitation of Motex Lanscope Endpoint Manager (CVE-2025-61932) delivering an updated Gokcpdoor, with Havoc C2 also used in some attacks [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: Bronze Butler targeting of Japanese enterprises
campaigns.summary: Secureworks reports spear-phishing and strategic web compromise against Japanese heavy industry, manufacturing and international relations organizations, including a Flash zero-day against SKYSEA Client View, and Daserf backdoor use.

campaigns.name: Daserf with steganography
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports Bronze Butler's Daserf backdoor variants using steganography, delivered mainly via targeted email.

campaigns.name: Pre-summit targeting of South Korea
campaigns.summary: FireEye tied TEMP.Tick to a malicious Word document in early May 2018 amid increased Chinese and Russian espionage against South Korea ahead of the Trump-Kim summit; success and exact victims were unclear.

campaigns.name: East Asian DLP software vendor compromise
campaigns.summary: ESET reports Tick compromised an East Asian DLP developer's update servers and trojanized third-party installers, reaching two customers; ESET notified the company in March 2021 per its Japanese post and published in March 2023. Initial access is unknown.

campaigns.name: Lanscope zero-day exploitation
campaigns.summary: Sophos CTU reports Bronze Butler exploited CVE-2025-61932 in Motex Lanscope Endpoint Manager as a zero-day (mid-2025) to deploy an updated Gokcpdoor; patches issued 2025-10-20 per press reports.

diamond.adversary: Chinese-assessed espionage actor tracked as TEMP.Tick, Tick and Bronze Butler [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Daserf, Netboy/Invader, ShadowPy, Ghostdown, Gokcpdoor, Havoc; spear-phishing, web compromise, software supply-chain compromise, zero-days [S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Encrypted C2 [S3]; compromised vendor update servers [S5]; internet-facing Lanscope servers [S6]. Specific C2 infrastructure not collected.
diamond.victim: Japanese industry and government, South Korean entities, and an East Asian DLP vendor with military and government customers [S2][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting Chinese interests regarding Japan and the Korean peninsula (analyst inference from targeting; FireEye's timing relative to the Trump-Kim summit) [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Widely deployed endpoint-management and security software in Japan (SKYSEA, Lanscope) and software update mechanisms [S3][S5][S6].

gaps: Could not open the primary FireEye 2018 report, Secureworks original, ESET and Sophos pages directly (fetch failures); facts rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage, so wording and dates should be verified.
CFR page content (names, sponsor, victims) was seen only in search snippets.
Exact FireEye cluster boundary for TEMP.Tick versus Tick/Bronze Butler is not confirmed; no MITRE group mapping is recorded in this record.
No government attribution (Japan, ROK, US) verified; claims of Japanese police or PLA unit attribution (e.g. Unit 61419 appears in Malpedia aliases) were not confirmed from a primary source.
Unit 42 reporting on Tick (USB air-gap malware, 2017) was seen but publication dates were not confirmed, so it is not cited.
Victims and impact of the 2018 Word document and the 2025 Lanscope campaign are not public in sources gathered.
Initial access vector for the DLP vendor compromise is unknown [S5].

CyberScoop (S2) snippets did not name TEMP.Tick or the Word document; those details rest on Korean-language press coverage (S8) and were not checked against FireEye's primary report. JPCERT/CC dates Lanscope zero-day exploitation to April 2025, versus Sophos's mid-2025.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is endpoint-management and DLP/security software and its update servers, plus Japan- and Korea-focused allied government and industry networks. STEP 2: The actor has a history of exploiting widely deployed regional enterprise software, including zero-days [S3][S6]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is spear-phishing or web compromise, then Daserf-class backdoor, or vendor/supply-chain compromise, then long-term collection [S3][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued intellectual-property and policy collection against Japanese and Korean industry and government. MDCOA is trojanized updates from a compromised security or management vendor reaching defense and military customers [S5]. Candidate indicators: anomalous behavior on endpoint-management servers, unexpected installers from vendor update channels, steganographic image downloads, and Word documents timed to diplomatic events [S2][S4][S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories for Japanese and Korean endpoint-management and security products used by partner and coalition networks. (2) Authorities: supply-chain and partner-network incidents may require host-nation and vendor coordination; confirm authorities before action. (3) Mission assurance: inventory where management and DLP agents run on mission systems and prepare update-channel verification and rollback. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied counterparts in Japan and the ROK and with DC3 where DIB software is involved.
